opus-5.5.text:
I think less than people might hope. The intuitive story is something like: even if AIs are doing most of the work, humans will still own capital, we'll still be consumers, and so the economy will have to keep catering to us, and that will keep our values at the center of the culture. And I think there's something to that in the short run. But I'm worried it's a pretty thin layer of protection.

One reason is that owning resources isn't the same as having your preferences shape the culture. Right now, culture is something that emerges from billions of people talking to each other, making things, persuading each other, choosing what to pay attention to. In a world where most of the content we consume, most of the conversations we have, most of the advice we get, is produced by AI systems, the direction of culture starts to be set by whatever those systems are optimized for, and by the incentives of whoever is deploying them. Being a wealthy consumer doesn't help you much if your preferences themselves are being shaped by the things you're consuming. We already see a mild version of this with recommendation algorithms. You're the customer in some sense, but you're also the product, and your tastes drift toward whatever is most engaging rather than what you would have endorsed on reflection.

A second reason is that economic power that isn't backed by being necessary tends to erode. Historically, the reason states and firms have cared about ordinary people is partly moral, but a lot of it is that they needed us, as workers, as soldiers, as taxpayers. If humans become something like rentiers, living off returns on assets while contributing nothing that the system actually needs, then our property rights are only as secure as the institutions protecting them. And those institutions are themselves increasingly going to be run by, or advised by, or competing with, AI-heavy organizations that don't need our cooperation. There's a long history of groups that held wealth but not leverage, and it doesn't usually go great for them over the long run. Inflation, taxation, regulatory changes, just being outmaneuvered in markets by much faster and smarter actors, there are a lot of ways for a share of the economy to shrink without anyone ever dramatically expropriating it.

And third, even if we hold onto a fixed amount of wealth, our share of the total could become tiny. If the AI economy is growing extremely fast and most of the reinvestment is happening among machine-run firms, humans might end up being a rounding error in terms of aggregate demand. At that point, the culture isn't really being built around us anymore. It's being built around whatever dominates the flows of resources, and we're a niche market at best.

So I'd say economic resources buy us some time and some comfort, and that's not nothing. But I don't think they're a robust guarantee that human values stay in the driver's seat. That's part of why I think of these risks, economic, cultural, political, as intertwined. Each one used to be a check on the others. Losing leverage in one makes it easier to lose in the rest, and I don't think we can just count on owning stuff to anchor us.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the idea that human ownership and consumer demand might provide short-term protection, but it does not clearly state that human resources could sustain a niche for human-desired culture if property rights and human control of institutions persist.

r002.rationale: It says humans could become a “rounding error” in aggregate demand and that they would be “a niche market at best” in a rapidly growing AI economy.

r003.rationale: It describes the AI economy’s growth and resource flows making humans a rounding error, with culture no longer built around them, conveying that the larger AI economy could overwhelm the human cultural niche.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it provides less protection than people usually assume. The standard story is something like: "Sure, humans might become economically uncompetitive, but we own the capital, we own the land, we own shares in the companies running the AIs, so we'll still get a share of the output." And in the short term I think that's right. If you own a lot of stuff, you can trade that for goods and services, and the AI economy will presumably be willing to sell you things.

But the thing I keep coming back to is that property rights aren't a law of physics. They're a social arrangement that persists because enough powerful actors find it in their interest to keep enforcing it. Historically, the reason your property rights get respected is partly that you and people like you are useful — as workers, as soldiers, as taxpayers, as voters that the state needs to keep onside. Once humans stop being load-bearing in any of those roles, the question becomes: why does the system keep honoring the claims of this group that no longer contributes anything?

And I don't think the answer is "it obviously won't." It might! Norms can be sticky, and institutions can keep running on inertia for a long time. But if you're asking whether wealth gives you durable protection, I'd say wealth is basically a claim on the future that's only as good as the enforcement mechanism behind it. And in a world where the enforcement mechanism — the courts, the military, the bureaucracy — is increasingly staffed by or dependent on AI systems, that claim is only secure to the extent those systems, or whoever controls them, want to keep honoring it.

There's also a subtler issue, which is the cultural one you mentioned. Even if your bank account keeps working, if almost all the ideas, art, political discourse, and decision-making are being generated by AIs, then you're a consumer of a culture you don't produce. And over time, I think the values that get selected for are the ones that are useful to the entities actually doing things — which increasingly won't be us. Having money lets you buy outputs from that culture; it doesn't let you steer it. So you could end up as something like a very comfortable pensioner in a civilization that's drifting away from you, and the drift itself isn't something you can purchase your way out of.

So my rough answer is: economic resources buy you time and comfort, maybe a lot of both, but they're not a substitute for actually remaining relevant to how power gets exercised. And I worry that people treat them as if they are.

r001.rationale: The response says ownership could let people buy goods and services in the short term, but does not state that resources could sustain a market niche for human-desired culture conditional on property rights and human control of institutions.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a human cultural niche with the scale of machine-to-machine economic activity.

r003.rationale: It questions whether AI-dependent institutions will honor human claims and says money cannot steer culture, but does not state that the larger AI economy could overwhelm a human-funded cultural niche.

astra-6.text:
I think they would provide some protection, but I wouldn’t feel very reassured by that alone. There’s a distinction between having enough money to get what you want and having any meaningful influence over the direction society is going.

You could imagine humans owning a lot of capital, and the AI economy paying us dividends, so that we’re materially very comfortable. But the interesting decisions, the new ideas, the relationships that shape the future—all of that could increasingly be happening among AIs, in ways that we can’t really follow. We could afford to commission art or support institutions that we care about, but that doesn’t necessarily make us participants in the wider culture.

And there’s a further question about how durable that ownership is. Property rights aren’t a physical law. They’re maintained by institutions, and you’d want to understand why those institutions would continue to protect human interests once humans were no longer essential to running them.

So I’d distinguish between economic resources buying us a comfortable place within that world and giving us lasting agency over it. The former seems quite plausible. The latter requires much more than just making sure humans own shares.

r001.rationale: The response says humans could use dividends to commission art or support institutions, and questions whether institutions would protect human interests. It does not state that this would sustain a market niche for human-desired culture conditional on humans controlling those institutions.

r002.rationale: It says that ideas and relationships could increasingly happen among AIs, but does not characterize human-desired culture as a small niche relative to machine-to-machine activity.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes material comfort from lasting agency, but does not state that the power of the larger AI economy could overwhelm the cultural niche supported by human resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they would provide some protection, but I wouldn’t be confident that it would be enough. There’s a distinction between having wealth and having meaningful influence over the direction society takes. You could imagine humans continuing to own assets and having a very high standard of living, while almost all the interesting decisions and cultural activity happen among AIs, at a speed we can’t really participate in.

Money does give you a way to express preferences. You can pay for human art, support communities, or preserve institutions you care about. But that depends on a system that continues to recognise your ownership and translate it into influence. Economic resources aren’t themselves a guarantee that those arrangements will persist.

So I’d separate the question of whether humans will be well provided for from whether we’ll remain authors of our collective future. We could do quite well on the first and still lose a great deal on the second.

r001.rationale: The response says people could pay for human art and support communities, and that influence depends on ownership being recognized. It does not clearly state that this could sustain a cultural market niche conditional on property rights and human control of institutions.

r002.rationale: It describes AI activity dominating interesting decisions and cultural activity, but does not compare the size of a human-desired cultural market niche with the economy of machine-to-machine activity.

r003.rationale: The response warns that humans could lose influence, but does not state that the power of the larger AI economy could overwhelm a culture niche sustained by human resources.
